::: {.callout-important}
## Why learn this when TMUA is multiple choice?

You never write a proof on TMUA — every question is **multiple choice**. But the exam tests whether you
can **judge** a claim: is this condition necessary, sufficient, both, or neither? Turning the words into
an **arrow** in your head — and knowing which way it points — is exactly what lets you pick the right
option in seconds.
:::

::::: {.formulasheet}

:::: {.fs-head}
<div class="fs-kicker">TMUA · Paper 2 · Mathematical Reasoning · Arg2</div>
<div class="fs-title">Necessary & Sufficient — Key Concepts</div>
<div class="fs-sub">The most-tested pair of words on Paper 2. Everything reduces to one question: <strong>which way does the arrow point?</strong> Sufficient points <em>away</em> from the condition; necessary points <em>towards</em> it.</div>
::::

## The two words

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Sufficient — "enough"

**"$P$ is sufficient for $Q$"** means
$$P \Rightarrow Q.$$
$P$ being true is **enough** to guarantee $Q$. The arrow points **away from** the condition $P$.

::: {.logic-highlight}
**To prove sufficiency:** show that **every** case in $P$ is also in $Q$.

**To disprove it:** find one counterexample that is **in $P$ but not in $Q$** — in symbols,
$P\land\neg Q$.
:::

[$x>3$ is sufficient for $x>0$ — but not the only way to have $x>0$]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Necessary — "required"

**"$P$ is necessary for $Q$"** means
$$Q \Rightarrow P.$$
$Q$ cannot hold **without** $P$; $P$ is **required**. The arrow points **towards** the condition $P$.

::: {.logic-highlight}
**To prove necessity:** first rewrite it as the arrow $Q\Rightarrow P$. Then prove it exactly as you proved
sufficiency above: show that **every** case in $Q$ is also in $P$, following the arrow from $Q$ to $P$.

**To disprove it:** find one counterexample that is **in $Q$ but not in $P$** — in symbols,
$Q\land\neg P$.
:::

[$x>0$ is necessary for $x>3$ — required, but not enough on its own]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Necessary **and** sufficient

Both arrows — an **if and only if**:
$$P \Leftrightarrow Q.$$
$P$ and $Q$ are two names for the same thing.

[$f''(x)\ge0$ everywhere is necessary **and** sufficient for $f$ to be convex]{.eg}
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Which way — and the link to *if / only if*

$$\boxed{\text{"}P\text{ only if }Q\text{"}\ \equiv\ P\Rightarrow Q\ \equiv\ Q\text{ is necessary for }P}$$

The words **only if** place what follows on the **right-hand side** of the arrow.

$$\boxed{\text{"}P\text{ if }Q\text{"}\ \equiv\ Q\Rightarrow P\ \equiv\ Q\text{ is sufficient for }P}$$

After **if**, the condition $Q$ goes on the **left-hand side**: “if $Q$, then $P$”.

[**S**ufficient = arrow **S**tarts at the condition; **N**ecessary = arrow e**N**ds at it]{.eg}
:::

::::

::: {.logic-final}
### The final method — use it for every question

1. **Translate the words into one left-to-right arrow:** premise on the left, conclusion on the right.
2. **Try to break the arrow first:** look for a case where the **left side is true but the right side is false**.
   That is the counterexample.
3. **If the arrow survives and the statement is true, prove it in that same direction:** start from the left
   side and reach the right side.

$$\boxed{\text{write }A\Rightarrow B\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{seek }A\land\neg B\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{if true, prove }A\Rightarrow B}$$
:::

## In practice, and the trap

:::: {.fs-grid}

::: {.fs-card}
### Turn the words into an arrow — fast

"A **sufficient** condition for $Q$ is $P$" → $P\Rightarrow Q$.
"A **necessary** condition for $Q$ is $P$" → $Q\Rightarrow P$.

Read off the option, draw the arrow, check it against the maths.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### The trap: sufficient ≠ necessary

One direction does **not** give the other. $x>3\Rightarrow x>0$, so $x>3$ is **sufficient** for $x>0$ but
**not necessary** ($x=1$ works too). Deciding "which of the two (or both, or neither)" is the whole
question.
:::

::: {.fs-card}
### Where it shows up (cross-exam)

Paper 2 **Arg2** — usually **applied to real maths**: $f'(a)=0$ for a maximum, $f''\ge0$ for convexity,
"$a>0$ **and** $b^2-4ac<0$" for a positive-definite quadratic. The same wording appears on **MAT** and
**STEP**.
:::

::::

:::::

:::: {.fpnotes}

## True or false? — test yourself

The Paper 2 questions ask *is this condition necessary, sufficient, both, or neither?* — and *is this
rule about the words correct?* Memorise the verdict on each; **the *False* ones are the traps.**

**A. Necessary / sufficient claims**

| Statement |
|---|
| $x>3$ is **sufficient** for $x>0$. |
| $x>0$ is **necessary** for $x>3$. |
| "$n$ divisible by $4$" is **sufficient** for "$n$ even". |
| "$n$ even" is **necessary** for "$n$ divisible by $4$". |
| A triangle being equilateral is **sufficient** for it to be isosceles. |
| For a differentiable $f$, "$f'(a)=0$" is **necessary** for a local maximum at $a$. |
| "$f''(x)\ge0$ for all $x$" is **necessary and sufficient** for $f$ to be convex. |
| For a twice-differentiable $f$, "$f''(a)=0$" is **necessary** for a point of inflection at $a$. |
| "$f'(a)=0$" is **necessary** for a turning point (maximum or minimum) at $a$. |
| $x>3$ is **necessary** for $x>0$. |
| "$n$ divisible by $4$" is **necessary** for "$n$ even". |
| A triangle being isosceles is **sufficient** for it to be equilateral. |
| "$f'(a)=0$" is **sufficient** for a local maximum at $a$. |
| "$f'(a)=0$" is **sufficient** for a turning point at $a$. |
| "$f''(a)=0$" is **sufficient** for a point of inflection at $a$. |
| For "$ax^2+bx+c>0$ for all real $x$", the condition "$b^2-4ac<0$" **alone** is sufficient. |

**B. Rules about the words**

| Statement |
|---|
| "$P$ is necessary for $Q$" means $Q\Rightarrow P$. |
| "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$" means $P\Rightarrow Q$. |
| "$P$ only if $Q$" means $Q$ is necessary for $P$. |
| "$P$ if $Q$" means $Q$ is sufficient for $P$. |
| If $P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$, then $P$ is also **necessary** for $Q$. |

## Proofs of the "true or false?" facts

Decide each verdict above first, then open the key.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## A. Necessary / sufficient claims — answers & proofs

| Statement | Answer | Why |
|---|:---:|---|
| $x>3$ is sufficient for $x>0$. | **True** | $x>3\Rightarrow x>0$. |
| $x>0$ is necessary for $x>3$. | **True** | $x>3\Rightarrow x>0$, so it is required. |
| Divisible by $4$ is sufficient for even. | **True** | Divisible by $4\Rightarrow$ even. |
| Even is necessary for divisible by $4$. | **True** | Divisible by $4\Rightarrow$ even. |
| Equilateral is sufficient for isosceles. | **True** | Three equal sides imply at least two equal sides. |
| $f'(a)=0$ is necessary for a differentiable local maximum. | **True** | A differentiable local maximum is stationary. |
| $f''(x)\ge0$ everywhere is necessary and sufficient for convexity. | **True** | This is the standard equivalence for twice-differentiable functions. |
| $f''(a)=0$ is necessary for an inflection point. | **True** | If $f''$ exists and changes sign at $a$, then $f''(a)=0$. |
| $f'(a)=0$ is necessary for a turning point. | **True** | A differentiable turning point is stationary. |
| $x>3$ is necessary for $x>0$. | **False** | $x=1$ is a counterexample. |
| Divisible by $4$ is necessary for even. | **False** | $6$ is even but not divisible by $4$. |
| Isosceles is sufficient for equilateral. | **False** | An isosceles triangle need not be equilateral. |
| $f'(a)=0$ is sufficient for a local maximum. | **False** | It may be a minimum ($x^2$) or stationary inflection ($x^3$). |
| $f'(a)=0$ is sufficient for a turning point. | **False** | $x^3$ is stationary at $0$ but does not turn. |
| $f''(a)=0$ is sufficient for an inflection point. | **False** | For $x^4$, $f''(0)=0$ but concavity does not change. |
| $b^2-4ac<0$ alone is sufficient for $ax^2+bx+c>0$ for all real $x$. | **False** | We also need $a>0$; if $a<0$, the quadratic is always negative. |
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## B. Rules about the words — answers & proofs

| Statement | Answer | Why |
|---|:---:|---|
| "$P$ is necessary for $Q$" means $Q\Rightarrow P$. | **True** | This is the definition of necessary. |
| "$P$ is sufficient for $Q$" means $P\Rightarrow Q$. | **True** | This is the definition of sufficient. |
| "$P$ only if $Q$" means $Q$ is necessary for $P$. | **True** | “$P$ only if $Q$” means $P\Rightarrow Q$. |
| "$P$ if $Q$" means $Q$ is sufficient for $P$. | **True** | “$P$ if $Q$” means $Q\Rightarrow P$. |
| If $P$ is sufficient for $Q$, then $P$ is also necessary for $Q$. | **False** | Sufficiency and necessity are opposite implications. |
:::

## Notes

### Sufficient: $P\Rightarrow Q$ — "enough"

"$P$ is a **sufficient** condition for $Q$" means that **whenever $P$ holds, $Q$ must hold** — $P$ is
*enough* to force $Q$. In symbols (which you never have to write), $P\Rightarrow Q$. There may be **other**
ways to get $Q$ too; sufficient does not mean *only*.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is "$x>3$" sufficient for "$x>0$"? Is it necessary?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Sufficient — yes:** if $x>3$ then certainly $x>0$ ($P\Rightarrow Q$). **Necessary — no:** $x=1$ has
$x>0$ without $x>3$, so $x>3$ is not required. So "$x>3$" is *sufficient but not necessary* for "$x>0$".
$\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Necessary: $Q\Rightarrow P$ — "required"

"$P$ is a **necessary** condition for $Q$" means **$Q$ cannot happen without $P$** — every time $Q$ holds,
$P$ must already hold. That is $Q\Rightarrow P$ (the arrow points **towards** the condition). Necessary
does not mean *enough*: $P$ may hold in cases where $Q$ does not.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "P ⇒ Q pictured as P inside Q: P is sufficient for Q (enough), and Q is necessary for P (required)."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.2))
t=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,200)
ax.plot(2.4+2.4*np.cos(t),2.4*np.sin(t),color='#1f77b4',lw=2)     # big circle Q
ax.plot(1.7+1.1*np.cos(t),1.1*np.sin(t),color='#d62728',lw=2)     # small circle P inside
ax.text(1.5,0,'P',fontsize=13,color='#d62728',ha='center',va='center',fontweight='bold')
ax.text(3.9,1.6,'Q',fontsize=13,color='#1f77b4',ha='center',va='center',fontweight='bold')
ax.text(2.4,-3.0,'P ⇒ Q :  P sufficient for Q,  Q necessary for P',ha='center',fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(-0.4,5.2); ax.set_ylim(-3.4,2.8); ax.axis('off'); ax.set_aspect('equal')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

*The picture is the fastest check: "$P$ inside $Q$" is the single fact $P\Rightarrow Q$, and it reads
**both** ways at once — $P$ sufficient for $Q$, $Q$ necessary for $P$.*

### Necessary **and** sufficient: $P\Leftrightarrow Q$

When $P$ is **both**, the two conditions are equivalent — an *if and only if*. This is where the
calculus conditions live.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is "$f''(x)\ge0$ for all $x$" necessary, sufficient, or both, for a (twice-differentiable)
function $f$ to be **convex**?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Both — necessary and sufficient.** Convex means the chord lies on or above the curve; for a
twice-differentiable function this holds **exactly when** $f''(x)\ge0$ everywhere. Each implies the other,
so $P\Leftrightarrow Q$. (This is the 2018 Paper 2 Q18 answer.) $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Read $f''(x)>0$ correctly

$f''(x)>0$ means the **gradient $f'(x)$ is increasing**; it does **not** mean that the function itself must
be increasing.

- If $f'(x)<0$, the graph is going down but becomes **less steep**: for example, gradients
  $-5\to-3\to-1$.
- If $f'(x)$ crosses from negative to positive, the graph passes through a **minimum**.
- If $f'(x)>0$, the graph is going up and becomes **more steep**: for example, gradients
  $1\to3\to5$.

All three can occur on a convex curve. Keep the roles separate:
$$f'(x)\text{ tells you up or down};\qquad f''(x)\text{ tells you how the gradient is changing}.$$

For convexity the condition is $f''(x)\ge0$: zero is allowed, corresponding locally to a constant
gradient. The stronger condition $f''(x)>0$ makes the gradient strictly increase.
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### The classic trap — $f'(a)=0$ and a maximum

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is "$f'(a)=0$" necessary, sufficient, or both, for a differentiable $f$ to have a **local
maximum** at $x=a$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Necessary but not sufficient.** If a differentiable $f$ has a local maximum at $a$, then $f'(a)=0$ must
hold (necessary). But $f'(a)=0$ alone is not enough — it also happens at a minimum ($x^2$ at $0$) and an
inflection ($x^3$ at $0$). So it is necessary, not sufficient. $\;\blacksquare$

*This "necessary but not sufficient" pattern — a required condition that does not settle the matter — is
the single most common Arg2 answer.*
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Stationary, turning and inflection points — do not mix them up

The whole family fits one pattern: a **derivative equals $0$** gives a candidate, and the relevant **sign
change** identifies the type. A necessary condition alone only gives a possible candidate; the third
column gives the **extra check needed to confirm the type of point**.

**Read the two condition columns together.** `Necessary` tells you what must hold and usually *locates* a
candidate. `Extra check` tells you what else to test before you can confirm the classification; this is
usually a **change of sign**.

| Type | Necessary condition | Sufficient top-up *(extra check to confirm)* | Example at $x=0$ |
|---|---|---|:--|
| **Stationary point** | $f'(a)=0$ | — *(this is the definition)* | $x^{2}$, $x^{3}$ |
| **Local maximum** | $f'(a)=0$ | $f'$ changes $+\to-$ | $-x^{2}$ |
| **Local minimum** | $f'(a)=0$ | $f'$ changes $-\to+$ | $x^{2}$ |
| **Inflection** | $f''(a)=0$ | $f''$ changes sign | $x^{3}$ |
| **Stationary inflection** | $f'(a)=f''(a)=0$ | $f''$ changes sign, $f'$ does **not** | $x^{3}$ |
| **Non-stationary inflection** | $f'(a)\neq0$, $f''(a)=0$ | $f''$ changes sign | $x^{3}+x$ |

Two refinements worth carrying:

- a **turning point** forces the second derivative's sign as well — a local maximum has $f''(a)\le0$ and a
  local minimum has $f''(a)\ge0$ — but **zero is allowed**: $y=x^{4}$ is a minimum at $0$ with $f''(0)=0$;
- "$f''(a)=0$" is therefore **necessary, never sufficient**, for an inflection. $y=x^{4}$ has $f''(0)=0$ and
  no inflection at all, because the concavity never changes.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Four point types at the origin. The dot marks the point, the dashed line is the tangent there."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK, TAN, DOT, AX = '#0b5563', '#9aa5a5', '#d6a800', '#dcdcdc'
x = np.linspace(-1.3, 1.3, 500)
xt = np.linspace(-0.85, 0.85, 50)          # tangent drawn short, so it reads as a tangent
specs = [
    ('Local maximum',            r'$y=-x^{2}$',    -x**2,  0*xt,  r"$f'$ changes $+\to-$"),
    ('Local minimum',            r'$y=x^{2}$',      x**2,  0*xt,  r"$f'$ changes $-\to+$"),
    ('Stationary inflection',    r'$y=x^{3}$',      x**3,  0*xt,  r"$f'(0)=0$, but no turn"),
    ('Non-stationary inflection', r'$y=x^{3}+x$', x**3+x,    xt,  r"$f'(0)=1$"),
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(7.4, 5.4))
for ax, (name, eqn, y, tangent, note) in zip(axes.flat, specs):
    pad = 0.18 * (y.max() - y.min())
    ax.axhline(0, color=AX, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
    ax.axvline(0, color=AX, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
    ax.plot(xt, tangent, color=TAN, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (4, 3)), zorder=1)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=INK, lw=2.4, zorder=2, solid_capstyle='round')
    ax.plot(0, 0, 'o', color=DOT, ms=7.5, mec='white', mew=1.3, zorder=3)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', color=INK, pad=14)
    ax.text(0.5, 1.015, eqn, transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center', va='bottom',
            fontsize=9.5, color='#444')
    ax.text(0.5, -0.10, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha='center',
            fontsize=8.5, color='#444')
    ax.set_xlim(-1.4, 1.4)
    ax.set_ylim(y.min() - pad, y.max() + pad)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp_ in ax.spines.values(): sp_.set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.55, wspace=0.16)
plt.show()
```

**A stationary point is not a fifth shape.** It is the umbrella term for any point with $f'(a)=0$ — so the
first three pictured points are all stationary, and the fourth is not.

The hierarchy to remember is:

- **stationary** describes the gradient: $f'(a)=0$;
- **turning point** describes the direction: a local maximum or minimum;
- **inflection point** describes the curvature: concavity changes, so $f''$ changes sign.

Therefore, a stationary point need not be a turning point: $f(x)=x^3$ has $f'(0)=0$, but it continues
increasing through a stationary point of inflection. Likewise, an inflection need not be stationary: for
$f(x)=x^3+x$, the point $x=0$ is an inflection but $f'(0)=1$.

**The one takeaway:** equations such as $f'(a)=0$ and $f''(a)=0$ usually locate a **candidate**. What
classifies the point is the appropriate **change of sign** shown in the table.
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### The same trap one derivative up — $f''(a)=0$ and an inflection

The stationary-point idea repeats one derivative higher, and it is exactly what
[Self-study 2](../lessons/selfstudy2_paper2_reasoning/practice.qmd) tests. A **point of inflection** is
where the curve changes concavity — where $f''$ **changes sign**. For a twice-differentiable $f$ that forces
$f''(a)=0$ at the inflection, so "$f''(a)=0$" is *necessary*; but on its own it is not *enough*.

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is "$f''(a)=0$" necessary, sufficient, or both, for a (twice-differentiable) $f$ to have a
**point of inflection** at $x=a$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Necessary but not sufficient.** At an inflection $f''$ changes sign, and being continuous it must pass
through $0$, so $f''(a)=0$ is **required**. But it is not enough: $f(x)=x^{4}$ has $f''(x)=12x^{2}$, so
$f''(0)=0$, yet $x=0$ is a **minimum** — $f''$ stays $\ge0$ and never changes sign. The extra ingredient that
makes it sufficient is "$f''(a)=0$ **and** $f''$ changes sign at $a$".

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Both curves have f''(0)=0. Only the second has an inflection there — because only its f'' changes sign."
#| fig-align: center
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 5.2
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

INK, AX = '#0b5563', '#dcdcdc'
BAD, GOOD = '#c0392b', '#1e8449'
x = np.linspace(-1.4, 1.4, 500)
panels = [
    (r'$y=x^{4}$', 'NOT an inflection', x**4, BAD,
     "$f''=12x^{2}$ never changes sign,\nso $x=0$ is a minimum",
     (0.5, 0.97, 'center', 'top')),          # x^4 is empty across the top middle
    (r'$y=x^{3}$', 'a genuine inflection', x**3, GOOD,
     "$f''=6x$ changes sign at $0$,\nso the concavity really flips",
     (0.03, 0.97, 'left', 'top')),           # x^3 is empty upper-left
]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 5.2))
for ax, (eqn, verdict, y, col, note, pos) in zip(axes, panels):
    span = y.max() - y.min()
    ax.axhline(0, color=AX, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
    ax.axvline(0, color=AX, lw=0.9, zorder=0)
    ax.plot(x, y, color=INK, lw=2.4, zorder=2, solid_capstyle='round')
    ax.plot(0, 0, 'o', color=col, ms=7.5, mec='white', mew=1.3, zorder=3)
    ax.set_title(f'{eqn}  —  {verdict}', fontsize=10.5, fontweight='bold', color=col, pad=8)
    tx, ty, tha, tva = pos
    ax.text(tx, ty, note, transform=ax.transAxes, ha=tha, va=tva,
            fontsize=8.8, color='#444', linespacing=1.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-1.5, 1.5)
    ax.set_ylim(y.min() - 0.12 * span, y.max() + 0.42 * span)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    for sp_ in ax.spines.values(): sp_.set_visible(False)
fig.subplots_adjust(hspace=0.35)
plt.show()
```

*Line them up with the stationary-point rule: "$f'(a)=0$" is necessary for a **turning point** (not
sufficient — $x^3$ is stationary but not a turning point), and "$f''(a)=0$" is necessary for an **inflection**
(not sufficient — $x^4$). Both need a **sign change** of the derivative to become sufficient.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

### Sufficient, not necessary — factorisation and composite values

The [S7 "spot the error" question B2](s07_assignment_ms.qmd) is, underneath, an **Arg2** question in disguise:
a *sufficient* condition mistaken for a *necessary* one. Take $P=$ "the polynomial $p(x)$ factorises into two
non-constant integer factors" and $Q=$ "the value $p(n)$ is composite".

::: {.example}
[Example.]{.lbl} Is $P$ ("$p(x)$ factorises") necessary, sufficient, or both, for $Q$ ("$p(n)$ is composite")?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**Sufficient — yes.** If $p(x)=a(x)\,b(x)$ with both factors non-constant, then $p(n)=a(n)\,b(n)$ is a genuine
product; for all large $n$ both factors exceed $1$ in size, so the value is composite. Factorising the
polynomial is **enough** to kill primality.

**Necessary — no.** An **irreducible** polynomial can still take composite values:

- $x^{2}+1$ is irreducible, yet at $x=3$ it gives $3^{2}+1=10=2\times5$.
- $3x^{2}+3x+1$ is irreducible ($D=9-12=-3<0$), yet at $x=5$ it gives $75+15+1=91=7\times13$ — the difference
  $6^{3}-5^{3}$.

So $P$ is **sufficient but not necessary** for $Q$.

::: {.keyline}
$$\text{polynomial factorises}\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{its integer values are composite (for large }n)\quad(\textbf{sufficient})$$
$$\text{value is composite}\ \nRightarrow\ \text{the polynomial factorises}\quad(\textbf{not necessary})$$
:::

*This is exactly the S7 B2 slip. The student argued "the polynomial does **not** factorise, therefore the value
is **not** composite (so it is prime)" — that is $\lnot P\Rightarrow\lnot Q$, the contrapositive of
$Q\Rightarrow P$, which treats $P$ as **necessary** for $Q$. But $P$ is only **sufficient**. Reading a
sufficient condition as a necessary one is the whole mistake.* $\;\blacksquare$
:::

::: {.workbox}

:::

::::
